# 🌍 Public API Data Analysis

You're the analyst on a **global market-expansion** team. Before the company commits budget to new regions, you need a quick, defensible read on three questions — and you'd rather pull **live public data** than wait on a vendor.

This workbook answers each with a **free, no-auth public API**:

- **How big is the opportunity?** — country populations from the **World Bank** to rank addressable markets
- **What are the operating conditions?** — live **weather** (Open-Meteo) for candidate hub cities, a proxy for logistics and field-ops planning
- **What's our treasury exposure?** — top **crypto** prices (CoinGecko) for a team that holds some digital assets on the balance sheet

Everything below runs against real endpoints over the MicroVM's 80/443 egress — no API keys, no secrets. Change the widgets and cells re-run live.

```mermaid
graph LR
  W["World Bank API"] --> M["Market size (population)"]
  O["Open-Meteo API"] --> C["Operating conditions (weather)"]
  G["CoinGecko API"] --> T["Treasury exposure (crypto)"]

  C --> B
  T --> B
```

## Step 1 · Size the markets — World Bank population

Market size starts with people. We pull the **2022 total population** for every country from the World Bank indicator API, drop missing values and micro-territories (< 1M), and rank the result. This `countries` table is our shortlist of where demand could plausibly scale.

import requests
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Fetch world population data from World Bank API (no auth needed)
resp = requests.get('https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?date=2022&format=json&per_page=300', timeout=15)
data = resp.json()[1]  # First element is metadata, second is data

countries = pd.DataFrame(data)
countries = countries[countries['value'].notna()].copy()
countries = countries[['country', 'value']].copy()
countries['country_name'] = countries['country'].apply(lambda x: x['value'])
countries['population'] = countries['value'].astype(float).astype(int)
countries = countries[['country_name', 'population']].copy()
countries = countries[countries['population'] > 1000000]  # Filter small territories
countries = countries.sort_values('population', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Fetched {len(countries)} candidate markets from the World Bank API")
countries.head(15)

## Step 2 · Rank the shortlist — top markets by population

A leadership-ready ranking. Drag **Top N** to widen or tighten the shortlist; the chart re-runs so you can frame the conversation around the 10 biggest markets or the top 40.

# @param {"type": "slider", "min": 5, "max": 50, "step": 5, "default": 20, "label": "Top N"}
top_n = 20
# Visualize the top N markets by population
topN = countries.head(top_n)
plt.figure(figsize=(12, max(4, top_n * 0.3)))
plt.barh(topN['country_name'], topN['population'] / 1e6, color='#89b4fa')
plt.xlabel('Population (millions)', color='#a6adc8')
plt.title(f'Top {top_n} Candidate Markets by Population (World Bank API, 2022)', color='white', fontsize=14)
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.xticks(color='#a6adc8')
plt.yticks(color='#a6adc8')
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.2, axis='x')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

## Step 3 · Read the operating conditions — live weather by hub city

Market size isn't the whole story — you also run people and product on the ground. We pull **current conditions** for a set of candidate hub cities from Open-Meteo. Temperature, wind, and humidity are a fast proxy for field-ops and logistics planning (cold-chain, outdoor install crews, warehouse HVAC load).

import requests
import pandas as pd

# Fetch weather data from Open-Meteo API (no key needed)
# Current conditions for candidate hub cities
cities = [
    {'name': 'New York', 'lat': 40.71, 'lon': -74.01},
    {'name': 'London', 'lat': 51.51, 'lon': -0.13},
    {'name': 'Tokyo', 'lat': 35.68, 'lon': 139.69},
    {'name': 'Sydney', 'lat': -33.87, 'lon': 151.21},
    {'name': 'Paris', 'lat': 48.86, 'lon': 2.35},
    {'name': 'Berlin', 'lat': 52.52, 'lon': 13.40},
    {'name': 'Mumbai', 'lat': 19.08, 'lon': 72.88},
    {'name': 'S\u00e3o Paulo', 'lat': -23.55, 'lon': -46.63},
]

weather_data = []
for city in cities:
    url = f"https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude={city['lat']}&longitude={city['lon']}&current=temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m,relative_humidity_2m"
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
    current = r.json()['current']
    weather_data.append({
        'city': city['name'],
        'temperature_c': current['temperature_2m'],
        'wind_speed_kmh': current['wind_speed_10m'],
        'humidity_pct': current['relative_humidity_2m'],
    })

weather = pd.DataFrame(weather_data)
print("Live operating conditions from Open-Meteo API:")
weather

## Step 4 · Compare conditions side by side

Three quick panels — temperature, wind, humidity — across the hub cities. Bars are colored by temperature band (blue = cold, green = mild, red = hot) so extremes that could complicate operations jump out at a glance.

# Plot weather comparison
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))

colors = ['#f38ba8' if t > 25 else '#89b4fa' if t < 10 else '#a6e3a1' for t in weather['temperature_c']]
axes[0].barh(weather['city'], weather['temperature_c'], color=colors)
axes[0].set_xlabel('\u00b0C', color='#a6adc8')
axes[0].set_title('Temperature', color='white')
axes[0].tick_params(colors='#a6adc8')
axes[0].axvline(0, color='#585b70', linewidth=0.5)

axes[1].barh(weather['city'], weather['wind_speed_kmh'], color='#cba6f7')
axes[1].set_xlabel('km/h', color='#a6adc8')
axes[1].set_title('Wind Speed', color='white')
axes[1].tick_params(colors='#a6adc8')

axes[2].barh(weather['city'], weather['humidity_pct'], color='#89dceb')
axes[2].set_xlabel('%', color='#a6adc8')
axes[2].set_title('Humidity', color='white')
axes[2].tick_params(colors='#a6adc8')

plt.suptitle('Live Operating Conditions Across Hub Cities (Open-Meteo API)', color='white', fontsize=14, y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

## Step 5 · Gauge treasury exposure — crypto prices

Finally, treasury. The company holds a slice of digital assets, so before expanding we sanity-check that book against the market. Pick a **reporting currency** and how many top coins to pull; CoinGecko returns live prices, market caps, and 24h moves. Use the **24h Change %** column as a fast volatility read on what we're carrying.

# @param {"type": "dropdown", "options": ["usd", "eur", "gbp", "jpy"], "default": "usd", "label": "Reporting currency"}
vs_currency = "usd"
# @param {"type": "slider", "min": 5, "max": 50, "step": 5, "default": 20, "label": "Number of coins"}
num_coins = 20

import requests
import pandas as pd

# Fetch cryptocurrency prices from CoinGecko (no auth)
resp = requests.get('https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/coins/markets', params={
    'vs_currency': vs_currency,
    'order': 'market_cap_desc',
    'per_page': num_coins,
    'sparkline': False
}, timeout=15)
crypto = pd.DataFrame(resp.json())[['name', 'symbol', 'current_price', 'market_cap', 'price_change_percentage_24h']]
crypto.columns = ['Name', 'Symbol', 'Price', 'Market Cap', '24h Change %']
print(f"Treasury check — top {num_coins} assets by market cap (reported in {vs_currency.upper()})")
crypto

## Wrap-up

In a few cells and three public APIs you've assembled the backbone of an expansion brief: a **ranked market shortlist** (World Bank), a **live operating-conditions** read for candidate hubs (Open-Meteo), and a **treasury exposure** snapshot (CoinGecko) — no credentials anywhere.

**Where to take it next**
- Join the population ranking to your own revenue-per-capita assumptions to turn size into a TAM estimate
- Pull Open-Meteo's forecast (not just current) to flag seasonal risk windows per hub
- Log the crypto snapshot to S3 on a schedule to build your own price history
